Who is a worker? And what do they deserve? These sound like legal questions. They are really questions about poverty.
The conference on New Forms of Employment, AI and Labour Rights today in Tbilisi brought together Georgian and European experts to wrestle with platform work, algorithm-driven hiring, and the future of labor protection. The debates were sharp. But what struck me most was how directly they connect to something I work on every day: poverty reduction in Georgia.

Here is the link that is not being made loudly enough.
The next phase of poverty reduction in Georgia runs through jobs — not just any jobs, but secure jobs with a floor of protection. And right now, that floor is missing for most Georgian workers.

Consider this. In 2024, only 46% of employed Georgians had paid annual leave. Only 44% had paid sick leave. And only 43% had pension insurance. More than half of Georgia's employed population is working without basic protections — self employment is simply the default.
Platform work — Bolt drivers, Glovo couriers, gig workers of all kinds — sits at the sharp end of this trend. Most opt for service contracts over employee status. The reason is straightforward: 1% personal income tax as a service contractor versus 20% as an employee. It is a rational choice.

A speaker from Lithuania made a point today that stayed with me: governments should not wait for courts to resolve what politicians need to decide. If the state sees a problem — and these numbers are a problem — it should act.
AI is accelerating the urgency. Lithuania's public employment services are already using it to profile job seekers and predict labor market outcomes. And the speed of disruption is outpacing policy: AI replaced translators in Lithuania not in the predicted five years — but in one.
For Georgia, these are not abstract future questions. They are arriving now.

Georgia's tax structure makes informality the rational choice for platform workers today. What would it take to flip that incentive — and make formal employment the better deal?

Succession planning: the most critical form of promotion.

Bernd was rolling out AI across African units of a global company. The contract had been a huge win for him, a mid-ranking partner in a large consultancy.

He and his young family had moved from Amsterdam to Pretoria for the work. His children now wanted to return home. His wife had set a deadline.

Christmas.

Bernd knew the client would ruin his reputation if he just cut and ran. Hence hiring me as his coach.

Our work together enabled him to sort the situation out. What he needed was a safe pair of hands to run the project instead of him.

Here is my distillation of the process Bernd implemented. It has helped a number of managing partners and business owners I have worked with since:

1) Do not appoint anyone who merely wants to move up. That ruled out Bernd’s assistants. Instead, identify people who are keen to do more senior work.

2) At an early stage, identify several potential candidates. One is too few. Five is the upper limit. Bernd identified two who ran in-country teams.


3) Develop and test candidates early. Bernd got one potential successor to roll out a beta version of the AI in two countries. The other was tasked with sorting out HR policies and communications across a region.

4) Minimise surprises. Bernd got feedback on how his guys were doing. One turned out to be indecisive. The other was inspirational. Bernd tentatively proposed his successor to the firm’s leadership.

Yes! He and his family returned to Europe.

The list above is even-numbered. That does not appeal to me aesthetically.

Is there a fifth principle here I can add? Share your ideas or suggestions in the comments.

Responsible AI sounds like a phrase that belongs in a corporate strategy document.
It belongs in your business, however small you are, however informally you are using AI tools.

Responsible AI is simply the practice of using AI in ways that are honest, safe, and fair. To your customers, to your team and to the people your business decisions affect.
That sounds straightforward. In practice, most businesses are not doing it because they don't know what it actually requires. Here are the four things it comes down to.

1. Knowing what your AI tools are doing with your data.
When you or your team paste information into an AI tool, a client name, a contract, financial details, that data goes somewhere. Most free and low-cost AI tools use your inputs to improve their models. That means sensitive information about your clients could be contributing to a system they never consented to. Responsible AI means knowing this before it becomes a problem.

2. Not presenting AI output as your own expert judgement without checking it.
AI tools hallucinate, a technical term for confidently producing information that is factually wrong. Hallucination rates across top AI models range from 22% to 94%. If you are using AI to write proposals, give advice, or communicate with clients and you are not reviewing the output before it goes out, you are putting your reputation on the line every single time.

3. Being transparent when AI is involved.
A Canadian airline's chatbot gave a customer incorrect information about a bereavement fare. The airline argued the chatbot acted independently. The court ruled the business was fully responsible for everything its AI communicated. Your customers have a right to know when they are interacting with or receiving outputs from an AI system and courts are increasingly agreeing.

4. Making sure your AI does not make decisions that should belong to a human.
Hiring decisions. Credit decisions. Customer service resolutions. These carry real consequences for real people. AI can inform them. It should not make them alone and unchecked.

Documented AI incidents rose from 233 in 2024 to 362 in 2025. Most of them were not caused by rogue technology. They were caused by businesses that moved fast and skipped the thinking. Responsible AI is not a framework you need a legal team to implement. It is a set of decisions about how you use the tools you already have and who is accountable for what they produce. That is where it starts.

What is one thing your business could do this week to use AI more responsibly?

An IISc professor recently walked into his advanced deep learning lecture, looked at the room, and did something rare: he threw the syllabus out the window.
He didn't touch the whiteboard. He didn't discuss neural network architectures. Instead, he asked a question that had clearly kept him awake the night before:
"Why did you bother coming to this class today?"
It wasn't a trick question. It was genuinely unsettling.
He confessed that he has stopped hiring student research assistants. Why wait on human bandwidth when he can spin up dozens of AI agents in parallel to test an idea in minutes? Humans, in his own lab, had become the bottleneck.
For generations, we operated on an unspoken contract: work hard, sharpen your intellect, master complex knowledge, and society will reward you. Our entire idea of meritocracy was built on cognitive scarcity.
Now, raw thinking is cheap. It’s an abundant utility.
When a student noted that an LLM is a better teacher anyway; infinitely patient, never irritable, tailoring analogies on the fly, the professor didn't get defensive. He agreed.
So why sit in a lecture hall at one of the country's premier research institutes?
His answer was a striking analogy: Universities are turning into gyms.
You can do push-ups at home for free. You don't need a gym membership to stay fit. Yet people pay for gyms because of the environment, the peer motivation, the accountability, and the forced discipline. In the near future, universities might not exist to distribute information. They’ll exist as physical spaces where people gather simply to keep their minds from atrophying.
The most jarring moment wasn't his warning about compute power consolidating into the hands of a few tech giants. It was watching a brilliant academic, someone at the absolute pinnacle of technical education, openly wonder what he should be teaching his own children to prepare them for what comes next.
If raw intelligence is commoditized, credentials and textbook retention won't protect anyone. What matters now is taste, the courage to ask the right questions, and the human connection that no model can simulate.
Gave me a lot to think about today.

The most persistent blind spot I see in GitOps is the assumption that it is only about applying YAML to Kubernetes clusters. In 2026, that framing is dangerously outdated. GitOps has become the decision audit trail for cloud infrastructure, and the teams still thinking in terms of manifests and sync waves are the ones getting blindsided.

The non-obvious shift is that GitOps is no longer just a deployment strategy. It has become the central nervous system for autonomous infrastructure operations. The latest industry data confirms that by 2026, GitOps extends far beyond Kubernetes. Pull requests are now the centerpiece for everything: infrastructure changes, security policy updates, automated validation, and AI-driven remediation. The winning teams are not the ones with the fastest Argo CD syncs. They are the ones that have designed their GitOps workflows so that every change, whether human-generated or AI-proposed, must pass through a pull request that enforces cost guardrails, compliance checks, and observability hooks before it ever touches production.

Another blind spot most platform teams miss is the rise of bidirectional GitOps. The common perception is that GitOps is a one-way sync from Git to infrastructure. The reality in 2026 is that the best platforms now reconcile changes made directly in the cloud back into the Git repository, creating a true source of truth that prevents drift. The teams that are winning are the ones that have embedded this reconciliation into their observability loop, so they can answer the question "did this manual override break the intended state" within seconds, not days.

For hiring managers and recruiting leaders: I do not just set up Argo CD or Flux. I design GitOps architectures that are built for autonomous operations, where the pull request is the governance contract between the operator and the business. I understand that GitOps in 2026 is not a tool you install. It is an operational model that requires designing the policy enforcement layer, the drift detection feedback loop, and the rollback strategy before the first repository is connected. If your team is struggling with AI-generated infrastructure changes that bypass manual review, cloud drift that creates silent inconsistencies, or a GitOps setup that cannot correlate a deployment with a business outcome, I can architect the solution.

The hardest question nobody is asking: When an AI agent opens a GitOps pull request at 3AM to remediate a detected security vulnerability, and that change passes every automated validation but introduces a subtle cost increase that only appears 48 hours later due to a misconfigured autoscaler, who is accountable for that tradeoff, and how do you audit the decision in the merge commit?

The global population is not simply “shrinking.”

But the workforce is changing — and not in the same way everywhere.

In many higher-income economies, populations are aging and working-age talent pools are beginning to contract.

At the same time, younger workforces continue to expand across other regions.

For technology companies, this creates a new challenge:

How do you keep building when the skills you need are no longer available in one location?

Here is what the demographic shift could mean for tech:

1️⃣ Competition for specialized skills will intensify

As experienced workers retire and fewer younger workers enter some labour markets, companies may face stronger competition for engineers, AI specialists, cybersecurity professionals, data experts, and technical leaders.

2️⃣ Automation will become a capacity strategy

AI and automation will not only be used to reduce costs.

They will help smaller teams handle repetitive work, improve productivity, and focus human expertise on decisions that require context, creativity, and accountability.

3️⃣ Products will need to serve older users

Aging populations will increase demand for accessible digital products, health technology, assistive tools, financial services, and interfaces designed for a wider range of physical and cognitive needs.

4️⃣ The workforce will become more age-diverse

Companies will need better systems for retaining experienced professionals, supporting continuous learning, and helping workers adapt as technologies and required skills change.

5️⃣ Talent strategies will become more global

When expertise is scarce locally, companies will increasingly need to recruit across regions, build distributed teams, and access specialists without requiring relocation.

6️⃣ Knowledge transfer will become business-critical

As senior professionals leave the workforce, undocumented technical and institutional knowledge can disappear with them.

Strong documentation, mentoring, succession planning, and structured handovers will become essential infrastructure.

The future is not simply about doing the same work with fewer people.

It is about combining human expertise, AI, automation, continuous learning, and global talent more effectively.

The companies that prepare early will not be limited by the size of one local hiring market.

They will build access to the skills they need — wherever those skills are located.

Is your talent strategy prepared for demographic change?

Or is it still built around an unlimited local supply of candidates?

We are hiring 4 x ASIC contractors on behalf of our customer 💡📢

The company is a seed-stage well funded San Francisco based startup applying modern AI to silicon’s biggest bottleneck: analog. We have openings for contract circuit and layout designers. The work is remote: we provide the machines, PDKs and EDA licenses. Start dates are project-based, starting now, with room to extend.
 
1. Analog/ Mixed-Signal Circuit Design (2 openings)
 
Design and verify high-speed ADCs and the analog front ends of ADC-based SerDes receivers in advanced FinFET nodes.
Typical blocks: SAR and time-interleaved SAR ADCs, comparators, sampling front ends and track-and-holds, reference and bias circuits, clock distribution and timing-skew calibration, CTLE/AFE and termination.
Looking for: industry tape-outs of high-speed ADCs or SerDes receivers in FinFET, plus hands-on transistor-level design and simulation through signoff, including post-layout. Cadence or Synopsys flows are both fine.
 
2. Analog/ Custom Layout Design (2 openings)
 
Lay out high-speed data converters and SerDes analog blocks in advanced FinFET nodes.
Typical work: matched and interleaved arrays, common-centroid and symmetric placement, high-speed clock and signal routing, parasitic-aware layout, EM/IR, and DRC/LVS signoff.
Looking for: industry tape-outs of ADC or SerDes layout in FinFET. Virtuoso or Custom Compiler experience is fine.

Please contact jobs@anysilicon.com with your CV.
